category.name: DevOps and Google Cloud
category.description: DevOps practices and Google Cloud architecture decisions: what each service is for and when to choose it.

cards.front: Which questions should you answer before changing a running Linux service?
cards.back: Which process owns the listener, which user runs it, where its configuration comes from, where its logs go, and what survives a restart. On systemd hosts, systemctl inspects the unit and journalctl -u <unit> shows its logs.

cards.front: What is the difference between git diff and git diff --cached?
cards.back: git diff shows unstaged changes: the working tree compared with the staging area. git diff --cached shows staged changes compared with the last commit, which is what git commit would record. Check both before committing.

cards.front: Why use git revert rather than git reset to undo a commit on a shared branch?
cards.back: git revert records a new commit with the inverse change, so history others have already pulled stays intact. git reset followed by a force push rewrites shared history and disrupts every other clone.

cards.front: A secret was committed and later deleted and added to .gitignore. Is it safe?
cards.back: No. Earlier commits, clones, logs and caches still contain it, and .gitignore only affects untracked files. Revoke or replace the secret first, investigate its use, then plan history cleanup separately.

cards.front: What does set -euo pipefail do in a Bash script?
cards.back:
• -e: exit when a command fails (with exceptions in conditionals and some control flow).
  • -u: treat expansion of unset variables as an error.
  • -o pipefail: a pipeline fails if any command in it fails, not just the last.

It does not replace explicit handling of expected errors.

cards.front: What makes a script safe to rerun?
cards.back: It produces the same end state each time: for example, mkdir -p succeeds if the directory exists, and output files are overwritten rather than appended. Inputs, required tools, side effects and outputs are explicit, expansions are quoted, and failure paths are checked. Test on a disposable target first.

cards.front: In what order should you troubleshoot a failing web request?
cards.back: Name resolution, then routing, then connection establishment, then TLS, then the HTTP application. A failure at one layer prevents the later layers from running, so start at the first one that fails.

cards.front: "Connection refused" versus a timeout: what does each usually suggest?
cards.back: A refusal is an active answer, usually meaning no listener on that address and port or an explicit rejection. A timeout can come from filtering, routing, an unavailable peer or a stalled application. Neither is diagnosed by ping, which only tests ICMP.

cards.front: How do TCP and UDP differ?
cards.back: TCP provides an ordered byte stream with retransmission. UDP provides individual datagrams with no built-in delivery or ordering guarantees; applications add what they need. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 commonly use TCP, and HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP.

cards.front: What does TLS protect, and what does it not decide?
cards.back: TLS authenticates the server through certificate validation (chain, expiry, hostname) and protects data in transit. It does not decide whether an authenticated user may access a particular record; that is application authorization.

cards.front: What do 4xx and 5xx status codes generally indicate?
cards.back: 4xx usually describes a client-side request or access problem, such as 404 Not Found or 401 Unauthorized. 5xx indicates a server-side failure along the serving path, such as 502 Bad Gateway from a proxy whose upstream is down. Check which component generated it.

cards.front: When is it safe to retry a request automatically?
cards.back: When repeating the work is safe, such as an idempotent read. Use timeouts, a retry limit and backoff. For state-changing requests like payments, use an idempotency key with server-side deduplication so a repeat does not apply twice.

cards.front: What is the difference between a type 1 and a type 2 hypervisor?
cards.back: A type 1 hypervisor runs directly on hardware (VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V). A type 2 hypervisor runs on a host operating system; VirtualBox is commonly described this way.

cards.front: Compare the VirtualBox NAT, bridged, host-only and internal network modes.
cards.back:
• NAT: outbound access; inbound usually needs port forwarding.
  • Bridged: the guest appears on the physical network and may be reachable by other devices.
  • Host-only: private network between host and guests, no external access through it.
  • Internal: guests talk to each other only; no host or external access through it.

Every enabled adapter adds reachability, so check them all.

cards.front: Why is a VM snapshot not a backup?
cards.back: A snapshot depends on the VM's own storage chain, so losing those files loses the snapshot too. Reverting also discards everything since it was taken. Keep important work and backups outside the disposable guest.

cards.front: When would you choose a Unix-domain socket over a TCP socket?
cards.back: When both processes run on the same host, such as a reverse proxy and its application. It avoids exposing a TCP listener, and file ownership and permissions restrict access. It still needs authorization, and container mounts affect who can reach it.

cards.front: Why does a TCP protocol need message framing?
cards.back: TCP is a byte stream: one write does not guarantee one read, so messages can be split or joined. Define boundaries with length prefixes, delimiters or an established protocol, and set timeouts and size limits.

cards.front: When should a queue consumer acknowledge a message?
cards.back: Only after the intended result is safely recorded. Brokers may redeliver, for example after a crash before acknowledgment or when an SQS visibility timeout expires, so consumers must be idempotent or deduplicate work.

cards.front: How do continuous integration, continuous delivery and continuous deployment differ?
cards.back:
• CI: small changes are integrated frequently and checked automatically.
  • Continuous delivery: every passing change produces a deployable artifact; production can wait for approval.
  • Continuous deployment: every change that passes the required checks goes to production automatically.

CI does not require production access.

cards.front: What does "build once, promote the same artifact" mean, and why does it matter?
cards.back: Build a versioned artifact once, record its digest, and deploy that exact artifact to test, staging and production, with environment configuration kept separate. Rebuilding per environment can produce something different from what was tested.

cards.front: Compare rolling, blue/green and canary releases.
cards.back:
• Rolling: replace instances in batches; old and new versions coexist.
  • Blue/green: prepare a second environment and switch traffic; needs extra capacity and shared-data compatibility.
  • Canary: expose a small cohort first; needs representative traffic and reliable stopping signals.

cards.front: When does an application rollback work?
cards.back: When the previous artifact is still available and the older version can read the current data and configuration. Backward-compatible migrations keep that true. Restoring a database to an earlier time is disaster recovery that can discard later writes, not routine rollback.

cards.front: What is the difference between a CI cache and a release artifact?
cards.back: A cache (such as downloaded dependencies) only speeds up jobs; a miss should change timing, never results. A release artifact is the versioned output that is published and promoted between environments.

cards.front: Why is a high coverage percentage not proof of good tests?
cards.back: Coverage shows which code ran during tests, not whether the tests assert meaningful behavior or catch failures. Test important behavior and failure paths, and review any threshold as the code changes.

cards.front: How do jobs and steps differ in a GitHub Actions workflow?
cards.back: Steps within a job run in order on the same runner and share its filesystem. Jobs run independently, often on separate runners, unless needs declares a dependency; they exchange files through artifacts or other explicit storage.

cards.front: Why is pull_request_target dangerous with untrusted code?
cards.back: It runs in the base repository's context, with access to secrets and a write-capable token. Checking out and running a contributor's code there (including install and test scripts) hands those privileges to that code.

cards.front: How do you safely use a pull request title in a run: step?
cards.back: Pass it through an env: variable and quote that variable in the script. Interpolating ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} directly into the script text lets a crafted title inject shell commands.

cards.front: Why pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA?
cards.back: Tags are mutable and can be moved to different code. A reviewed full commit SHA identifies fixed content; update pins deliberately.

cards.front: What does id-token: write allow, and what limits it?
cards.back: It allows a job to request an OIDC identity token. The cloud provider's trust policy decides which workflows may exchange that token for a role, and the role's permissions limit what it can do. It replaces long-lived access keys.

cards.front: What must be decided before starting a canary?
cards.back: The stable baseline, the initial cohort, the measurements (error rate, latency, resource use, a product signal), the observation window, and the stopping rules. Keep enough stable capacity to take traffic back.

cards.front: What are the limits of a canary release?
cards.back: It reduces exposure while evidence is collected but cannot guarantee safety for rare failures, destructive data changes, or background jobs that bypass the traffic split. Both versions must also work with the same data and messages.

cards.front: What are the four OpenGitOps principles?
cards.back: Desired state is declarative, versioned and immutable (with history), pulled automatically by agents, and continuously reconciled with the actual state.

cards.front: What is drift in GitOps, and how should emergency changes be handled?
cards.back: Drift is a difference between the declared configuration and the running system; the controller reports or corrects it according to policy. Emergency manual changes must be captured in the source of truth, or reconciliation may undo them.

cards.front: What does reverting a GitOps configuration commit not do?
cards.back: It does not undo database writes, restore deleted data, or prove the earlier application supports the current schema. Verify health after reconciliation and use the recovery plan for data loss.

cards.front: How should browser code get access to cloud storage?
cards.back: Never with the server's cloud credentials. The server can issue a limited mechanism such as a signed URL with explicit authorization and expiry. Website customers have application identities, not cloud IAM users.

cards.front: How do authentication and permission differ for a workload calling a cloud API?
cards.back: Authentication proves the identity (for example, a workload role or OIDC-federated CI job). Permission decides what it may do; a valid identity can still be denied by its policies, resource policies, network rules or database authentication.

cards.front: What do you manage under IaaS, PaaS and SaaS?
cards.back:
• IaaS: the guest OS and application on provider VMs and networks.
  • PaaS: application behavior, data, configuration and access; the provider runs more of the runtime.
  • SaaS: configuration and use of a finished application.

Serverless still has quotas, failure modes, costs and configuration.

cards.front: What is the difference between a region and an availability zone?
cards.back: A region is a geographic deployment area. Availability zones are separate locations within a region that limit the impact of some failures. Multiple zones improve availability; multiple regions add decisions about replication, routing and recovery.

cards.front: Compare block, file and object storage.
cards.back:
• Block: disks attached to a machine.
  • File: shared filesystems mounted by several machines.
  • Object: objects addressed by key over an API, suited to uploads and static assets.

cards.front: Does a cloud budget alert stop spending?
cards.back: Generally not; it notifies people when spending crosses a threshold rather than enforcing a hard limit. Combine it with ownership tags and reviews of idle resources, egress and logging costs.

cards.front: What is the Terraform working cycle?
cards.back: Write configuration with pinned provider and module versions, run terraform init, check with terraform fmt -check and terraform validate, run terraform plan -out=tfplan, review it, then terraform apply tfplan. Confirm the account and environment first.

cards.front: Why is Terraform state treated as sensitive operational data?
cards.back: State maps resource addresses to real objects and can contain credentials, even for outputs marked sensitive. Store it in a remote backend with access controls, encryption, versioning and locking, and keep it and saved plans out of Git.

cards.front: What does removing a resource from Terraform state do?
cards.back: It stops Terraform managing the object; it does not delete the remote resource. To adopt or refactor resources, use supported import and move mechanisms instead of editing state JSON.

cards.front: Do Terraform CLI workspaces separate environments securely?
cards.back: They separate state instances but do not create an access-control boundary. Give environments separate state and credential boundaries, and avoid one large state shared by unrelated teams.

cards.front: Which tool category handles each lifecycle stage?
cards.back:
• Provision infrastructure: Terraform, CloudFormation.
  • Build machine images: Packer.
  • Configure an OS: Ansible, Puppet, Chef, Salt.
  • Build and run containers: Docker, Podman.
  • Orchestrate containers: Kubernetes.
  • Coordinate delivery: GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab CI.
  • Reconcile desired state: Argo CD, Flux.

cards.front: Why must two controllers not own the same setting?
cards.back: They overwrite each other continually, for example Terraform resetting an instance count that an autoscaler changed. Define which tool owns each setting and which differences are expected.

cards.front: How does a container differ from a VM?
cards.back: A container is an isolated process environment that shares the kernel of its runtime environment. A VM runs its own guest kernel on virtual hardware. Containers are not limited to one process, though separating responsibilities helps.

cards.front: Why record an image digest instead of a tag for a release?
cards.back: A tag can be reassigned to a different image, so it is not a fixed artifact identity. The digest identifies exact content and makes the release reproducible.

cards.front: What happens to data written inside a container's writable layer?
cards.back: It disappears when the container is removed. Use a volume or an external service for databases and uploads, and back that storage up; a volume is not a backup.

cards.front: Compare readiness, liveness and startup probes.
cards.back:
• Readiness: whether the workload should receive traffic.
  • Liveness: whether to restart it.
  • Startup: gives a slow-starting app time before other probes apply.

A liveness probe that checks a dependency can turn its outage into repeated restarts.

cards.front: What do a Kubernetes Deployment and Service each provide?
cards.back: A Deployment manages a set of replicated Pods and rolls out updates. A Service selects Pods by label and gives them a stable name and address so clients do not track individual Pods.

cards.front: How do metrics, logs and traces differ?
cards.back: Metrics summarize measurements over time (counts, latency distributions). Logs record individual events with context. Traces connect the operations of one request across several components.

cards.front: What are SLIs, SLOs and error budgets?
cards.back: An SLI measures a result, such as the fraction of valid requests that succeed. An SLO sets a target and window, such as 99.9% over 30 days. The error budget is the allowed shortfall: 1,000 failures per 1,000,000 eligible requests at 99.9%.

cards.front: Why keep metric labels bounded?
cards.back: Each distinct label combination creates a separate time series, so values like user IDs or arbitrary paths explode storage and cost. Put per-request detail in restricted logs or traces.

cards.front: What are the steps of a small incident workflow?
cards.back: Confirm impact and start time; assign coordination and investigation; mitigate with a known action such as stopping a rollout; verify recovery with user-facing evidence and communicate; record a timeline and follow-up actions with owners.

cards.front: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
cards.back: Authentication establishes an identity. Authorization determines what that identity may do. Network reachability is not proof that a request should be accepted.

cards.front: Why does a cloud role's trust policy matter as much as its permissions?
cards.back: Permissions define what the role can do; the trust policy decides who may assume it. Broad trust lets unintended identities obtain even narrow permissions.

cards.front: What lifecycle details should be documented for each secret?
cards.back: Who owns it, how it is issued, how applications receive and reload it, and how to revoke or replace it. Test rotation with dependent services so a change does not cause an outage.

cards.front: What is expand-and-contract for schema changes?
cards.back: A way to change a schema while old and new versions coexist: add a compatible field, deploy code that can use it, backfill safely, switch reads, and remove the old field only after older versions no longer depend on it.

cards.front: Why does a replica not replace backups?
cards.back: Replication reduces downtime from hardware or zone failures, but it copies accidental deletion and corruption too. Backups provide an independent history to restore from.

cards.front: What do RPO and RTO mean?
cards.back: Recovery point objective (RPO): the acceptable data loss, measured in time. Recovery time objective (RTO): how long restoration may take. An RPO of 15 minutes and RTO of one hour need recent recoverable data and a restore that fits within an hour.

cards.front: What is the 3-2-1 backup rule?
cards.back: Keep three copies of data, on two different storage types, with one copy off-site. It keeps copies out of the original failure domain; add immutable or offline copies when the threat model requires it.

cards.front: What does a restore drill involve?
cards.back: Pick a recovery point and its copies and keys, restore into a separate environment, validate data with a compatible app version, check workflows and integrations, measure recovery time and data gap, then document cutover and clean up. Keep destructive background jobs disabled.

cards.front: How does point-in-time recovery differ from an application rollback?
cards.back: A rollback deploys a previous artifact and keeps current data. Point-in-time recovery reconstructs data at an earlier time, so later writes may be lost; on Amazon RDS it creates a new instance that the application must be switched to.

cards.front: What does an idempotent Ansible task do on a second run?
cards.back: It converges on the desired state and reports no new change when the host already matches. Prefer state-describing modules over shell commands that run unconditionally.

cards.front: What should happen before automating a small company's servers?
cards.back: Inventory each server's purpose, owner, services, dependencies, jobs and data, back up and confirm a restore, then automate one low-risk task on a test machine before expanding in small batches.

cards.front: Why separate a web app from its scheduler before scaling?
cards.back: Each web replica would run the scheduled task, so three replicas run a cron job three times. Run the scheduler or worker separately and design jobs to tolerate retries; even Kubernetes CronJobs are not exactly-once.

cards.front: What must be recorded to reproduce a model?
cards.back: Training code revision, dataset version or immutable reference, feature transformations, parameters, dependencies, random seeds and evaluation results, stored with the model artifact and its promotion history.

cards.front: How do data drift, concept drift and training-serving skew differ?
cards.back:
• Data drift: the input distribution changes.
  • Concept drift: the relationship between inputs and the intended outcome changes.
  • Training-serving skew: features are processed differently in training and inference.

Input drift is a warning, not proof predictions got worse.

cards.front: Why might rolling back a model require more than restoring the weights?
cards.back: The model depends on compatible feature code and schema expectations. Retain a known-good artifact together with those, and define a fallback for when inference or input validation fails.

cards.front: What are the six sections of the Professional Cloud Architect exam guide, and which carries the most weight?
cards.back: Designing and planning a cloud solution architecture (about 25%, the largest), managing and provisioning a solution infrastructure, designing for security and compliance, analyzing and optimizing technical and business processes, managing implementation, and ensuring solution and operations excellence. Some questions refer to fictional case studies; the v6.1 guide lists Altostrat Media, Cymbal Retail, EHR Healthcare and KnightMotives Automotive.

cards.front: What are the levels of the Google Cloud resource hierarchy?
cards.back: Organization (tied to a Cloud Identity or Workspace domain), optional nested folders, projects, and resources. Every resource belongs to exactly one project. Policies set on a node are inherited by everything below it.

cards.front: Why can't a project administrator remove a role that was granted on the parent folder?
cards.back: IAM allow policies are additive: effective access is the union of bindings on the resource and all its ancestors. A lower level cannot subtract an inherited grant. Use a deny policy, narrow the folder grant, or move the project.

cards.front: How does an organization policy differ from IAM?
cards.back: IAM decides who may perform an action on a resource. An organization policy decides what configurations are allowed below a node, for every principal, using constraints such as resource locations, domain restricted sharing, or disabling service account key creation. Both are inherited, and organization policies can be tested in dry-run mode.

cards.front: Which organization policy constraints commonly appear in architecture designs?
cards.back:
• gcp.resourceLocations to restrict where resources are created.
  • iam.allowedPolicyMemberDomains (domain restricted sharing) to limit IAM grants to approved identities.
  • Disabling service account key creation.
  • Restricting external IPs on VMs, requiring OS Login, and skipping the default network.

cards.front: What is the difference between labels, tags and network tags?
cards.back: Labels are key-value metadata used for cost attribution and filtering; they appear in billing export but do not control access. Resource Manager tags are organization or project-level resources bound to resources, inherited, and usable in IAM conditions, organization policy conditions and firewall policies. Network tags are an older VM attribute used only by VPC firewall rules and routes.

cards.front: How do projects and Cloud Billing accounts relate?
cards.back: A billing account pays for many projects, but each project links to at most one billing account. Billing Account Administrator manages the account, Billing Account User allows linking projects to it, and Project Billing Manager allows changing a project's link.

cards.front: What are the three types of IAM roles, and when do you use each?
cards.back:
• Basic (Owner, Editor, Viewer): very broad; avoid in production.
  • Predefined: maintained by Google per service; the default choice, picking the narrowest that works.
  • Custom: your own permission list at organization or project level, when no predefined role is narrow enough; you maintain it.

cards.front: What are IAM Conditions used for?
cards.back: They restrict a role binding by attributes such as request time, resource name prefix, resource type or tags. Typical uses are access that expires automatically and access limited to resources carrying a specific tag.

cards.front: How do IAM deny policies and principal access boundary policies differ from allow policies?
cards.back: Only allow policies grant access. Deny policies attach to resources and block listed permissions regardless of allow grants, with optional exceptions; they are checked first. Principal access boundary policies attach to sets of principals and limit which resources those principals are eligible to access.

cards.front: Why should you avoid service account keys, and what replaces them?
cards.back: Keys are long-lived secrets that can leak and need rotation. Use attached service accounts on Google Cloud compute, Workload Identity Federation for GKE in clusters, Workload Identity Federation for AWS, Azure or OIDC/SAML workloads such as GitHub Actions, and impersonation for administrators. Use a key only when nothing else works.

cards.front: What permission is needed to attach a service account to a VM or Cloud Run service?
cards.back: iam.serviceAccounts.actAs on that service account, granted by the Service Account User role. It stops anyone who can deploy from borrowing a more powerful service account's permissions.

cards.front: What is the difference between Workload Identity Federation and Workforce Identity Federation?
cards.back: Workload Identity Federation lets external workloads (CI systems, other clouds) exchange their own tokens for short-lived Google credentials. Workforce Identity Federation lets human users from an external identity provider access Google Cloud without being synced into Cloud Identity.

cards.front: How do employees sign in to Google Cloud with existing Active Directory accounts?
cards.back: Google Cloud Directory Sync provisions users and groups from Active Directory or LDAP into Cloud Identity, and SAML single sign-on sends authentication to the existing identity provider so passwords stay there. Workforce Identity Federation is an alternative that avoids syncing.

cards.front: How can operators SSH to VMs that have no external IP addresses without a bastion host?
cards.back: Use Identity-Aware Proxy TCP forwarding: IAP checks the user's identity and IAM permissions, then tunnels the connection to the VM's internal address. OS Login ties Linux SSH access to IAM identities instead of per-VM keys.

cards.front: What is global and what is regional in a Google Cloud VPC network?
cards.back: The VPC network is global; subnets are regional. VMs in different regions of the same VPC reach each other over internal IPs without VPNs or peering, subject to firewall rules.

cards.front: Why use custom mode rather than auto mode VPC networks in production?
cards.back: Auto mode creates a subnet in every region from fixed ranges in 10.128.0.0/9, which often overlap with on-premises or other networks. Custom mode lets you plan non-overlapping ranges, including GKE secondary ranges, before connecting networks.

cards.front: What firewall rules exist in a new custom VPC, and how are firewall policies layered?
cards.back: Only implied rules: allow all egress and deny all ingress, at the lowest priority. Hierarchical firewall policies on the organization and folders are evaluated first, then network firewall policies and VPC firewall rules on the network. Rules are stateful, and targeting by service account is stronger than by network tag.

cards.front: When would you choose Shared VPC over VPC Network Peering?
cards.back: Choose Shared VPC when a central team should administer subnets, routes and firewalls while application teams in the same organization keep their own projects. Choose peering to connect a few independently administered VPCs, including across organizations. Peering is not transitive and needs non-overlapping ranges.

cards.front: How do Private Google Access, Private Service Connect and private services access differ?
cards.back:
• Private Google Access: a subnet setting so internal-only VMs reach Google APIs.
  • Private Service Connect: an internal IP endpoint in your VPC for Google APIs or a published service; works across organizations and with overlapping ranges.
  • Private services access: VPC peering with a Google-managed producer network, used by services such as Cloud SQL.

cards.front: What does Cloud NAT do, and what does it not do?
cards.back: It gives private VMs, GKE nodes and serverless egress outbound internet access without external IPs. It is a regional, managed service configured on a Cloud Router, with no NAT VM. It does not accept unsolicited inbound connections and is not needed for Google APIs when Private Google Access is enabled.

cards.front: How do HA VPN, Dedicated Interconnect, Partner Interconnect and Cross-Cloud Interconnect differ?
cards.back:
• HA VPN: IPsec over the internet with BGP; quick to set up; 99.99% SLA in supported topologies.
  • Dedicated Interconnect: your own physical circuits at a colocation facility for high bandwidth.
  • Partner Interconnect: through a service provider when you cannot reach a facility or need less capacity.
  • Cross-Cloud Interconnect: dedicated links to another cloud provider.

cards.front: Is Cloud Interconnect traffic encrypted, and which topologies give 99.9% and 99.99% SLAs?
cards.back: It is private but not encrypted by default; add MACsec or HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect. 99.9% needs two connections in one metro on different edge availability domains; 99.99% needs four connections across two metros and two regions.

cards.front: How do Google Cloud and on-premises resolve each other's private DNS names?
cards.back: A Cloud DNS forwarding zone sends queries for on-premises domains to on-premises resolvers. An inbound server policy gives on-premises resolvers an address in the VPC to query Cloud DNS private zones. DNS peering shares zones between VPCs.

cards.front: How do you choose between Application and Network Load Balancers?
cards.back: Application Load Balancers are layer 7 proxies for HTTP and HTTPS, with URL routing, Cloud CDN (global external) and Cloud Armor. Network Load Balancers handle TCP, UDP and other protocols: proxy variants terminate connections and can offload TLS, while passthrough variants preserve the client IP and support UDP.

cards.front: When would you choose a regional external Application Load Balancer over the global one?
cards.back: When TLS termination and request processing must stay in one region, for example for data residency, or when the application serves one region and uses the Standard Network Service Tier. The global version terminates at Google's edge worldwide and needs the Premium tier.

cards.front: What does Cloud Armor provide, and where does it attach?
cards.back: Security policies on backend services of external Application Load Balancers and some Network Load Balancers: preconfigured WAF rules based on the OWASP Core Rule Set, IP and geography rules, rate limiting and bot management. Cloud Armor Enterprise adds Adaptive Protection and further DDoS features.

cards.front: How do you choose between Compute Engine, GKE and Cloud Run?
cards.back: Compute Engine when you need OS or kernel control, licensed software or lift and shift. GKE when you need Kubernetes: Standard for node control, Autopilot to avoid node management. Cloud Run for stateless containers with the least operations, including scale to zero.

cards.front: What do managed instance groups provide that unmanaged instance groups do not?
cards.back: Identical VMs from an instance template, autoscaling, autohealing based on application health checks, rolling updates and canaries, regional distribution across zones, and stateful configuration. Unmanaged groups only group dissimilar VMs for load balancing.

cards.front: When should you use Spot VMs, and what is the trade-off?
cards.back: For fault-tolerant, restartable work such as batch processing, rendering and CI runners. They are heavily discounted but can be reclaimed at any time with short notice. Unlike legacy preemptible VMs, they have no maximum runtime.

cards.front: What is the difference between GKE Standard and GKE Autopilot?
cards.back: In Standard you manage node pools and pay per node. In Autopilot, Google manages nodes, enforces hardened defaults and bills for the resources Pods request. Autopilot is the usual starting point unless you need node-level control.

cards.front: What is the difference between Cloud Run services, jobs and worker pools?
cards.back: Services handle requests, scale with traffic including to zero, and split traffic between revisions. Jobs run containers to completion, optionally as parallel tasks. Worker pools run long-lived background workloads that do not serve requests, such as pull-based queue consumers.

cards.front: What are Cloud Run functions, and how are they triggered?
cards.back: The current name for Cloud Functions: deploy source code for one function, built and run on Cloud Run. They respond to HTTP requests or to events delivered by Eventarc from sources such as Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub and Cloud Audit Logs.

cards.front: What are the Cloud Storage classes and their minimum storage durations?
cards.back: Standard (none), Nearline (30 days), Coldline (90 days) and Archive (365 days). All share the same API and millisecond latency; colder classes cost less to store but more to retrieve, and early deletion is charged up to the minimum.

cards.front: When would you use Autoclass instead of lifecycle rules?
cards.back: Use Autoclass when access patterns are unknown or vary per object; it moves each object between classes based on its own access. Use lifecycle rules when the policy is known in advance, such as "Coldline after 90 days, delete after five years".

cards.front: What are the Cloud Storage location types?
cards.back: Region for the lowest latency to compute in that region, dual-region for two specific regions with optional turbo replication, and multi-region for a large geographic area. Dual-region and multi-region survive a regional outage.

cards.front: How do you protect Cloud Storage objects from deletion and modification?
cards.back: Object versioning keeps noncurrent versions after overwrites and deletes, soft delete keeps deleted objects recoverable for a period, and a retention policy locked with Bucket Lock enforces write-once-read-many. Object holds block deletion of individual objects.

cards.front: How does Hyperdisk differ from Persistent Disk, and which Hyperdisk types exist?
cards.back: Hyperdisk provisions capacity, IOPS and throughput separately and is recommended where supported. Types: Balanced (general), Balanced High Availability (synchronous across two zones), Extreme (highest IOPS), Throughput (analytics, cold data) and ML (read-only to many instances). Persistent Disk remains for series without Hyperdisk support.

cards.front: Which database fits which requirement?
cards.back:
• Cloud SQL: regional MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server.
  • AlloyDB: PostgreSQL-compatible, higher performance, mixed analytics.
  • Spanner: relational, strongly consistent, horizontal and multi-region.
  • Bigtable: wide-column, high-throughput time series and IoT.
  • Firestore: serverless documents for mobile and web.
  • Memorystore: in-memory cache.
  • BigQuery: analytics warehouse.

cards.front: What is the difference between Cloud SQL high availability and read replicas?
cards.back: High availability keeps a synchronous standby in another zone of the same region with automatic failover, protecting against zone failure. Read replicas are asynchronous, can be in other regions, scale reads, and can be promoted manually for disaster recovery.

cards.front: When is Spanner the right answer, and when is it over-engineering?
cards.back: Choose it when a relational workload needs strong consistency, horizontal write scaling or multi-region writes with very high availability; multi-region configurations use the Enterprise Plus edition. For a regional application that fits one primary, Cloud SQL or AlloyDB is simpler and cheaper.

cards.front: What determines Bigtable performance?
cards.back: Row-key design. Rows are sorted by key, so keys that start with a timestamp or sequential value create hotspots. Lead with a well-distributed value, such as a device ID, followed by a timestamp. Bigtable has no joins or multi-row transactions.

cards.front: When would you choose Dataflow over Managed Service for Apache Spark (formerly Dataproc)?
cards.back: Dataflow for new batch or streaming pipelines written in Apache Beam, with serverless autoscaling, windowing and exactly-once processing. Managed Service for Apache Spark to migrate existing Spark or Hadoop jobs with few changes, ideally on short-lived clusters or serverless batches reading from Cloud Storage.

cards.front: What was Vertex AI renamed to, and how should you approach AI requirements in a design?
cards.back: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (the v6.1 exam guide still says Vertex AI). Prefer pre-trained APIs or hosted models from Model Garden before custom training. Model Armor screens prompts and responses, and Sensitive Data Protection keeps sensitive data out of training sets and prompts.

cards.front: What is the difference between RTO and RPO?
cards.back: The recovery time objective is how long a service may be unavailable after a failure. The recovery point objective is how much recent data may be lost, measured in time. Agree both with the business before choosing a design.

cards.front: What are the cold, warm and hot disaster recovery patterns?
cards.back:
• Cold (backup and restore): backups only, infrastructure rebuilt from code; hours to days.
  • Warm standby: a scaled-down copy with replicated data in another region; minutes to hours.
  • Hot (active-active): full capacity in several regions; near-zero RTO and RPO, highest cost.

cards.front: How do zonal, regional and multi-regional designs differ?
cards.back: Zonal designs stop if their zone fails. Regional designs (regional MIGs and GKE clusters, Cloud SQL high availability, synchronously replicated disks) survive a zone outage. Multi-regional designs (global load balancing, Spanner multi-region, dual- or multi-region buckets) survive a region outage at higher cost.

cards.front: What does Backup and DR Service add over ad hoc snapshots?
cards.back: Central management of backups for Compute Engine, databases and other workloads, with backup vaults that keep copies immutable and protected from deletion during retention, even by compromised administrators. Keep backups in a separate project and location, and test restores.

cards.front: When do you use default encryption, CMEK, Cloud EKM and CSEK?
cards.back:
• Default: no specific key-control requirement.
  • CMEK: you must control rotation, disabling and destruction in Cloud KMS.
  • Cloud EKM: keys must stay outside Google in an external key manager.
  • CSEK: rare; keys supplied per request, Cloud Storage and Compute Engine only.

cards.front: What is the difference between Cloud KMS and Secret Manager?
cards.back: Cloud KMS holds cryptographic keys and performs operations with them; the key material does not leave it. Secret Manager stores secret values, such as passwords and API keys, as versions that applications read at runtime with per-secret IAM.

cards.front: What problem does VPC Service Controls solve that IAM does not?
cards.back: Data exfiltration with valid credentials. A service perimeter blocks Google API access to services such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery across its boundary, so data cannot be copied to projects outside it. Access levels and ingress or egress rules allow exceptions, and dry-run mode tests a perimeter first.

cards.front: What do Security Command Center and Binary Authorization do?
cards.back: Security Command Center finds misconfigurations, vulnerabilities and threats across an organization and reports compliance against benchmarks such as CIS. Binary Authorization enforces deploy-time policy on GKE and Cloud Run so that only attested images, for example signed by CI, can run.

cards.front: What are the four types of Cloud Audit Logs?
cards.back:
• Admin Activity: configuration changes; always on, cannot be disabled.
  • Data Access: reads and user-data access; off by default except BigQuery.
  • System Event: Google system actions; always on.
  • Policy Denied: denials by security policies such as VPC Service Controls.

cards.front: How do you retain audit logs for years in a tamper-resistant way?
cards.back: The _Required bucket keeps Admin Activity and System Event logs for a fixed 400 days. For longer retention, create an organization-level aggregated sink to a Cloud Storage bucket with a locked retention policy, or to BigQuery for analysis.

cards.front: How do you enforce data residency and regulatory controls on Google Cloud?
cards.back: Use the resource locations organization policy and regional resources. Assured Workloads creates folders with a control package (for example FedRAMP, CJIS or EU data boundary controls) that enforces locations, allowed services and personnel access controls. Compliance remains shared: certified infrastructure does not make a configuration compliant.

cards.front: What are log sinks and aggregated sinks used for?
cards.back: The Log Router evaluates sinks that send matching log entries to log buckets, BigQuery, Cloud Storage, Pub/Sub or another project. An aggregated sink at organization or folder level, with child projects included, centralizes logs from every current and future project. Exclusion filters drop low-value logs to control cost.

cards.front: Which Google Cloud tools answer which observability questions?
cards.back:
• Cloud Monitoring: metrics, dashboards, uptime checks, SLOs and alerting.
  • Cloud Logging: log storage, routing, log-based metrics and Log Analytics.
  • Error Reporting: grouped application exceptions.
  • Cloud Trace: latency across services in a request.
  • Cloud Profiler: CPU and memory hotspots in code.

cards.front: What do Cloud Build, Artifact Registry and Cloud Deploy each do?
cards.back: Cloud Build runs build steps in containers from triggers, with private pools for private network access. Artifact Registry stores container images and packages, including remote repositories that cache upstream sources; Container Registry is shut down. Cloud Deploy promotes releases through targets with approvals, canaries and rollback.

cards.front: Which infrastructure as code options does Google Cloud offer today?
cards.back: Terraform with the Google provider is the standard. Infrastructure Manager runs Terraform with managed state and execution. Config Connector manages Google Cloud resources as Kubernetes objects. Cloud Deployment Manager reached end of support in March 2026.

cards.front: How do sustained use discounts and committed use discounts differ?
cards.back: Sustained use discounts apply automatically to some older series (such as N1, N2, N2D and C2) that run for much of the month; E2 and newer series are not eligible. Committed use discounts require a 1- or 3-year commitment and give larger discounts; usage covered by a commitment does not also receive sustained use discounts.

cards.front: When would you choose a spend-based flexible commitment over a resource-based commitment?
cards.back: Choose spend-based when total spend is predictable but usage moves between regions, machine series, GKE and Cloud Run. Choose resource-based for a known amount of vCPUs, memory or GPUs in one region.

cards.front: Do budgets stop spending?
cards.back: No. Budgets send notifications at thresholds of actual or forecast spend, by email or Pub/Sub. For a hard limit, use quotas or automation triggered by the budget's Pub/Sub messages, such as stopping resources.

cards.front: How do you reduce BigQuery costs?
cards.back: On-demand pricing charges per data scanned, so partition and cluster tables, select only needed columns, set maximum bytes billed and estimate with bq query --dry_run. For steady heavy use, editions bill slot capacity with autoscaling, and Enterprise or Enterprise Plus commitments add discounts. Long-term storage pricing applies automatically after 90 days unmodified.

cards.front: Which network traffic costs money on Google Cloud?
cards.back: Ingress is free. Egress between zones and between regions is charged, and internet egress costs more. The Standard Network Service Tier is cheaper than Premium but supports only regional load balancers. Co-locate chatty components and use Cloud CDN for cacheable content.

cards.front: What are the 6 Rs of migration?
cards.back: Rehost (lift and shift), replatform (lift and optimize with managed services), refactor or re-architect (change the application), repurchase (replace with SaaS), retire (switch off), and retain (keep where it is for now).

cards.front: Which Google Cloud tool fits which migration task?
cards.back:
• Migration Center: discovery, utilization and TCO reports.
  • Migrate to Virtual Machines: VMs from vSphere, AWS or Azure to Compute Engine.
  • Google Cloud VMware Engine: run VMware workloads unchanged.
  • Database Migration Service: continuous database migrations to Cloud SQL or AlloyDB.
  • Storage Transfer Service: online object and file transfers.
  • Transfer Appliance: offline bulk transfer.

cards.front: How do you decide between Storage Transfer Service and Transfer Appliance?
cards.back: Estimate the online transfer time: data size in bits divided by usable bandwidth. 100 TB over a fully used 1 Gbps link takes about nine days. If that does not fit the schedule, ship a Transfer Appliance; otherwise use Storage Transfer Service, which also supports scheduled incremental syncs from S3, Azure and on-premises.

cards.front: What are the pillars of the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework?
cards.back: Operational excellence; security, privacy and compliance; reliability; cost optimization; performance optimization; and sustainability. Cross-pillar perspectives, such as AI and ML and financial services, apply the pillars to specific workloads.

cards.front: What process helps answer scenario questions on the exam?
cards.back: Identify business and technical requirements, then the constraints that eliminate options ("minimal operational overhead", "without code changes", "must stay in the EU"). Choose the simplest managed service that meets them, and reject any answer that ignores a stated constraint, adds unneeded components or breaks least privilege.

cards.front: Which traps appear most often in Professional Cloud Architect answer options?
cards.back: Basic roles, service account keys, self-managed products where a managed one fits, global services when the requirement is regional residency, detection-only controls (alerts, logs) when prevention is required, and extra services that solve a problem the question does not have.
